# Synthetic teaching note: choosing between structural models

This note is a synthetic fixture written for the PharmAgent test suite. It is not
taken from any book or paper.

## 1 Objective function and information criteria

Two nested structural models are commonly compared by the drop in the objective
function value. For one additional parameter a decrease of about 3.84 points
corresponds to a five percent significance level under the likelihood ratio test,
and a decrease of 6.63 points corresponds to one percent. Non-nested models are
compared with an information criterion such as the Akaike information criterion
(AIC), which penalises each extra parameter by two points.

## 2 Small differences are not decisive

A difference in AIC of less than two points between the best model and the
runner-up does not distinguish the two models statistically. In that situation
the simpler model is usually preferred, and the ambiguity should be reported rather
than hidden behind a single "best" label. Parsimony, mechanistic plausibility and
the intended use of the model all weigh more than a fraction of an AIC point.

## 3 Convergence and precision

A model that is selected while some subjects or the population run failed to
converge is not a reliable winner. Check the condition number of the covariance
matrix: a value above one thousand suggests over-parameterisation or poor
identifiability. Relative standard errors above fifty percent on a structural
parameter mean the data barely inform it, and fixing or removing the parameter is
often the honest choice.

## 4 Diagnostics beyond the number

Information criteria summarise fit; they do not show where a model fails. Always
pair the criterion with goodness-of-fit plots and a predictive check before
declaring a structure adequate.
